summary_plain: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) investigates the burning and extinction behavior of isolated liquid fuel droplets, such as heptane and methanol, in microgravity aboard the International Space Station. Researchers study how different ambient oxygen levels, pressures, and gaseous suppressants affect flame extinction and flammability limits. This research is critical for improving spacecraft fire safety and designing more effective, efficient fire suppression systems.
summary_expert: Conducted inside the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) using the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) on the ISS, FLEX examines spherically symmetric combustion of liquid droplets ranging in size from 1 to 5 mm in ambient environments of up to 40 percent oxygen by volume at pressures spanning 0 to 3 atm. Variables investigated include ambient pressure, oxygen mole fraction, diluent type, and suppressant mole fractions (using CO2, He, SF6, and N2), alongside slow convective flow tests. Key outcomes include the identification of both radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets, a limiting oxygen index (LOI) significantly lower than in normal gravity or previous predictions, and the discovery of stable, quasi-steady cool flames forming after the radiative extinction of the visible hot flame.

key_findings.text: The experiments have identified both the radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets.
FLEX identified a limiting oxygen index (LOI) that is both significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted and anticipated.

The most significant observation from these experiments is the identification of stable, quasi-steady cool flames that form after radiative extinction of the visible flame for heptane droplet combustion.

Research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity, implying that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.

earth_applications: Fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft
More efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems reducing the risk of toxic byproducts
Advanced combustion engines for improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions in automotive and industrial applications
